title: Inner Gold, Part 1: Why did Zen take root in the West?
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the question of why Zen took root in the West, opening a sesshin talk with Wendell Berry's poem "The Real Work." Nomon weighs suffering, charismatic teachers, and reverse Orientalism as answers, then turns to Robert A. Johnson's book Inner Gold, which describes projecting our own gold onto another person to carry for a while. Nomon tells of a physician who says Nomon "has the glow," and reads Johnson's story of hero-worshiping a cousin's husband, Thor, on a boyhood squirrel hunt. Nomon ends by wondering whether students and teachers in the lineage have been exchanging gold all along.

sentences.text: *This little piece by Wendell Berry keeps coming into my mind, called "The Real Work."
It may be that when we no longer know what to do, we have come to our real work, and that when we no longer know which way to go, we have come to our real journey.
The mind that is not baffled is not employed.*
Good afternoon, everybody.
The impeded stream is the one that sings.
The mind that's not baffled is not employed.
The impeded stream is the one that sings.
We don't always like to be impeded, but I guess that's how we sing.
So we create this interesting little situation called sesshin so that we can sing.
It seems to be like the more complicated, the better.
More impediments and more singing.
So I appreciate the many efforts that are happening that this could even be going on.
Especially Connie and Talus setting it up and planning it.
Both Bobs and John and everybody else in the kitchen.
Susan and her crew jumping in to try to serve the food.
We've not done the full service, serving the food with servers, for a long time, maybe five years or something like that, nearly than we did once.
So it's amazing.
It's amazing we can do all this.
So I hope you feel at least a little bit baffled.
Because if we only knew everything that was going on and it was only comfortable and nice, I guess that would be a pleasant way to spend the weekend.
Nothing wrong with that.
But maybe we really wouldn't be actualizing our real work if it was all super smooth, simple.
Probably could have had a caterer.
Or just ordered takeout.
The theme of the practice period this year is Zen pioneers.
We've been looking at a sampling of the individuals, early Zen priests and teachers, Japanese and Western people both, who were instrumental in Zen practice taking root here.
At least as far as we can tell in retrospect.
And lately I've been wondering anew why it worked.
Why was anyone in North America actually that interested?
I was just thinking about my own first direct exposure to Zen and that sense of bigger possibilities that I kind of felt but didn't understand.
I never would have felt it if there hadn't been many, many people before me to create the center that I walked into.
Was that all it was?
Was it just some sense in American life that there was something missing in our material-based lives?
It's not like we didn't already have spirituality of various forms and poetry and the other arts.
There are so many different ways to meet that sense of things being a little too narrow or constricted.
Why this particular version of an Asian tradition?
Why did that appeal to people?
So was that why?
Or often we say that the real motivation for practice is suffering.
And that's true enough.
I think we all want to find a way to be more comfortable in our skin, to not suffer, to be more okay, to have some support for even the possibility that maybe we're enough exactly as we are.
And our practice does seem to help with that.
It does seem to help as a skillful response to suffering, but it's so slow and it's so subtle.
That's why it's the rule rather than the exception to have somebody like Norman, this morning, say, "Well okay, 30 years in we're getting a bit of a flavor here."
That's good.
So it's hard to imagine that, as a response to suffering, Zen practice really was that compelling.
What would support the first American students of Zen to hang in there long enough?
And to get through the ways that this practice, in the subjective, evaluative way that we use, absolutely will make you feel worse, not better.
Get you more in touch with some of your unacknowledged sides.
And especially the genius plan that we have, that it's always done in the community.
So then you're bumping up against other people's, whatever you want to call it.
So it doesn't seem like a sense of limitation or materialism in our culture is enough of a motivation to do something this rigorous in this long form.
Our suffering doesn't seem like quite enough.
So was it the teachers themselves?
Some of the early teachers by all accounts were quite charismatic, quite skilled.
Suzuki Roshi apparently was mostly really charming.
I've heard plenty of stories of him being angry and difficult, so not 100%.
And if we zoom out to some of the other Buddhisms that were appearing in America in the 60s and 70s, I think of Chögyam Trungpa Rinpoche.
I know direct students of his, and they all say the same thing, that it was just magnetic.
He came in the room, everybody felt it.
Maybe they didn't know what they were feeling, but they felt something.
So was it that sense of magnetism or charm or charisma or the intelligence of the teachers?
Was that what allowed Zen to plant itself?
Or was it their foreignness?
In a cultural moment when Western culture seemed flat and incomplete and uninteresting, was it the Asian-ness, or at least the idea of the Asian-ness of these teachers, that appealed so strongly?
Did the first Western Zen students essentially fall in love, deeply in love, with some idea of Asian culture and spirituality as embodied in these teachers?
Sociologists talk about the denigration of Asian culture, the chop suey kind of stuff, as Orientalism, and that it runs both ways.
There's an idealization of Asian culture, which is reverse Orientalism.
So maybe it was reverse Orientalism, people who were just bowled over by the Japanese-ness of these teachers.
The other thing to remember is that it didn't work at first.
Early in the practice period, a little before, we did a little study of some of the earliest Zen pioneers in the 1900s and the 1930s, when it didn't actually go anywhere.
Some of the Japanese priests just packed up and went home.
Some of them just implanted themselves patiently in the culture and had to wait 20 years.
Remember we studied Nyogen Senzaki, who worked as a hotel clerk for 20 years until he finally decided maybe he could give a lecture.
I have a little pride arise sometimes that we've had more or less continuous practice for, I don't know, 24, 25 years, but I don't know if I would have been willing to wait 20 years first.
So anyway, it didn't really land at first.
So maybe some change in American culture had to happen, maybe these seeds had to be planted early on.
So it's a curious thing, why did it work?
We have some feeling for this now, but what if there was no one in the room who had any experience and we're all brand new to this, would we even be sticking around?

In parallel with having this curiosity about the planting of Zen in the West, I've been really curious about some of the things I'm experiencing in the last three or four or five years, as I've been engaged in planting another kind of Dharma here that's called mindfulness.

It's another form of Buddhism, a contemporary science Buddhism, where instead of talking about Buddha, we talk about fMRI machines and we cite people with doctorates and read a few poems and talk about psychology, but it's in fact very much the same thing somehow.
What I've noticed is a tremendous amount of excitement and energy on the one hand, from some of the people that I'm working with in the mindfulness classroom or the big mindfulness retreats.
I've had a couple of occasions where I've gone to the University of Washington and done a retreat with a great big room, 100, 150 people, and lots of interest in who I am and what this is all about.
And that's interesting.
Why is this planting itself?

In that project I've also noticed some strife and conflict, and I've had some surprisingly difficult challenges understanding and working with some of the other mindfulness pioneers down in the Seattle area.
So that makes me wonder, did these Zen pioneers actually get along?
Did they like each other?
They were mostly on their own, it seems like.
There was a little bit in the history about Nyogen Senzaki having strong feelings about a Japanese teacher in New York, and they didn't like each other.
Sokei-an.
So there seems to be a powerful interpersonal energy that arises, that focuses itself around individuals when whatever this is gets started.
It's interesting too that mostly what's recorded and remembered now about the Suzuki Roshis and the Maurine Stuarts and the Nyogen Senzakis is how much people really loved these teachers.
How much they learned from them.
The stories get told over and over again.
There's a certain kind of gathering from San Francisco Zen Center that's famous for this, where they tell the same Suzuki Roshi stories that they always tell.
So one wonders if that's the whole story.
Probably there is more strife and suffering in there too.
When we were looking at Zen pioneers we did look at the powerful and uncompromising work of a Western woman teacher, an English woman, who came to be known as Jiyu Kennett Roshi.
There are definitely some stories of challenge around her.
And it was interesting when we were reading her words, we felt a little edgy.
We were like, oh gosh.
She seems wise, but I don't know if I'd want to be hanging around with her.
So there were some powerful forces in people somehow as this unfolded.
What's it all about?
What was happening?
It makes me think about the introduction to *Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind*, which as you probably know is the most published book in English on Buddhism by far.
A gazillion million reprintings or editions.
In the introduction, Richard Baker very approvingly quotes Trudy Dixon, who is the editor and compiler of the book.
Sadly, she didn't live to see its publication.
She died of cancer, I think, right as it was going to press.
And Trudy Dixon wrote this about Suzuki Roshi.
In fact, she was writing about Suzuki Roshi, but she somehow felt like she had enough information to generalize about roshis in general.
So this is interesting.
Let's listen to this.
*Roshi is a person who has actualized that perfect freedom, which is the potentiality of all human beings.
He exists freely in the fullness of his whole being.
The flow of his consciousness is not the fixed repetitive pattern of our usual self-centered consciousness, but rather arises spontaneously and naturally from the actual circumstances of the present.
The results of this in terms of the quality of his life are extraordinary.
Buoyancy, vigor, straightforwardness, simplicity, humility, serenity, joyousness, uncanny perspicacity, and unfathomable compassion.
His whole being testifies to what it means to live in the reality of the present.
Without anything said or done, just the impact of meeting a personality so developed can be enough to change one's whole way of life.*
So that's pretty cool.
And I think now in 2016 we kind of say, oh, that's nice.
But it seems a little over the top to us.
Maybe a little silly.
Maybe a little unrealistic.
But I think in 1970 it seemed self-evidently true.
That that was the quality of the roshi, of the Zen master, the enlightened master.
And if we all tried hard enough and were skillful enough, maybe we could approach that level of perfection.
This seems like it had positive and negative qualities we've talked about before.
On the positive side, those guys were motivated.
They practiced devotedly, practiced hard.
On the negative side, it seems like maybe their communities and the teachers were set up for lots of trouble.
Many dramatic things happened in the 70s in almost every major Zen community in America.
Some major ethical breach involving a teacher.
So now maybe we'd call this projection and bias, and mostly that seems like a negative.
It seems unskillful.
It seems like giving away our power.
It seems a little destructive.
And really unfortunate.

And in this disempowered state, when we have made ourselves dependent on the other, like the Zen master, to validate us, we kind of have nowhere to go but to seek approval and be held in a holding pattern forever.
But recently I learned about another way of thinking about projection and interaction between students and spiritual teachers for sure, and maybe universally between all human beings.
An interesting model of projection which, when understood and managed wisely, is very positive.
Freeing, empowering.
I ran into a little book which I want to share with some of you in this talk and tomorrow, by a Jungian psychologist named Robert A.
Johnson.
Do you know about Robert A.
Johnson?
I didn't know about him, but maybe everyone knows about Robert A.
Johnson.
I always figure that when I find something cool.
Probably I just didn't know about this.
*Inner Gold: Understanding Psychological Projection.* Robert A.
Johnson, and there's a lot of Robert Johnsons, you've got to put the A in if you look him up.
Another Robert Johnson is the famous blues singer who sold his soul to the devil in exchange for musical virtuosity.
And as a result died young and created incredible music, but that's another story.
Anyway, Robert A.
Johnson turns out to really have been interesting too.
Born I think in the 20s, I didn't write down.
He was an early full-on Jungian.

Went to Zurich and studied with Emma Jung, Carl Jung's wife, and did therapy with Fritz Kunkel, or analysis they call it, Fritz Kunkel and Marie von Franz, who as I understand it were very important early Jungians.
Very highly regarded.
Before all that, Robert Johnson somehow ran into Krishnamurti in California and studied with him for some years.
Then he put all that together in some way and worked as a conventional psychologist, I guess, seeing clients for 20 years.
Having grown up non-religious, through the Jungian work he got interested in spirit and symbolism and all of mythology and all of this.
He ended up ordaining as a Benedictine monk.
Stopped and ended his career and lived four years in a Benedictine monastery in California, I think.
Then he emerged again.
Took up psychology again and started writing books in the 60s.
And I think he's still living but I think no longer very active.
So here's what Robert Johnson has to say about projection.
I'm really finding it really interesting and valuable, so I hope you feel the same.
And if not, I hope your impeded stream sings nicely.
This isn't the dharma talk I signed up for.
Where's the koans?
*My first analyst, Fritz Kunkel, said that there are many ways to learn psychology.
Read Greek mythology, read Jung, or watch.
Watching is best.
I learn so much from watching.
And one of the things I observe most carefully is the exchange of inner alchemical gold.*
Inner alchemical gold.
So gold like the metal.
*Inner gold is the highest value in the human psyche.
It is our soul, the self.
The innermost part of our being.
It is us at our best.
Our 24 karat gift to ourselves.
Everyone has inner gold.
It isn't created, but it does have to be discovered.
When I speak about gold this way, I'm also speaking about God.*
So we could say Buddha nature, I think, pretty safely.
Our inner gold.
*There are two ways to describe this mystery.
When we awaken to a new possibility in our lives we often see it first in another person.*
That's essentially his whole argument.
*When we awaken to a new possibility in our lives we often see it first in another person.
A part of us that has been hidden is about to emerge.
But it doesn't go in a straight line from our unconscious to becoming conscious.
It travels by way of an intermediary, a host.
We project our gold onto someone and suddenly we're consumed with that person.
The first inkling of this is when the other person appears to be so luminous that he or she glows in the dark.
That's a sure sign that something is changing in us and that we are projecting our gold onto another person.*
About three weeks ago I was starting a mindfulness class with a group of physicians.
I always ask people what their intentions are and why they're here.
One of them, a high-ranking physician, listed off all the things he does.
He could list it off really quickly.
He looks up at me and says, "The reason why I'm here is because Tim has the glow.
I somehow know that something's missing in my life.
I want to understand the glow."
So: inner gold, projected on me.
Having just read this book, it was so helpful to be able to say to myself, and to him, okay, I don't have to get worried about this or excited about this or feel like I'm something special.
Oh, I have the glow.
Oprah, here I come.
But just to recognize that here is another human being about to realize something about himself.
Right?
Projecting his inner gold.
I just happened to be in the right seat to receive it.
*When we observe the things that we attribute to the other person, we see our own depth and meaning.
Our gold goes first from us to them.
Eventually, it will come back to us.
Projecting our inner gold offers us the best chance for an advance in consciousness.*
So that's a strong statement.
Projecting our inner gold offers us the best chance for an advance in consciousness.
So he's not saying, work hard in your practice, is he?
That there's an exchange that maybe needs to happen.
So you can see the thesis I'm leading to here around our Zen pioneers.
Pretty obvious.
Is it that those young people, mostly pretty young, saw in the Suzuki Roshis their inner gold, something they were about ready to understand about themselves?
Now Robert Johnson gives a back story about his idea.
*In the Middle Ages, the work of alchemy was to produce gold from base metals.
There were charlatans trying to make actual gold.
But the best alchemists were those working with the gold of the spirit.
Alchemy comes from a time when the medieval mind was at its highest flowering.
In medieval times, people did not divide reality into inner or outer.
Or even ignore the difference between the two.*
And this seems to have been really true in medieval Asia as well.
Not this material thought, inner outer split that we have.
*For them, the inside and the outside were the same.
To accomplish all that we have today, we've had to split the world in two.
We've had to split the world in two.
We wouldn't be this competitive if we had a medieval mind.
But the price we pay for our accomplishments is loneliness and the inability to love.
Separation.
Love, we are our beloved.
I spent many years trying to help people differentiate between inner and outer.
You are you and I am I.
Your husband is your husband.
We still have not yet completed the transition to the modern mind.
Many psychological problems are a failure to differentiate between out there and in here.*
So that's interesting.
He's saying on the one hand we've lost some possibility from this integrated medieval mind.
On the other hand, we really aren't quite modern either.
So we're sort of stuck in between.
*According to the teachings of India, the external world is Maya, illusion.
It is considered illusory because it is actually within, not out there.
We see only the 10,000 things that we project.
In ancient China, Lao Tzu dreamed of a butterfly.
In his life, he didn't know whether he had dreamed the butterfly or the butterfly had dreamed him.
In the West, gold is the symbol of the self.
While in the East, the symbol of our inner divinity is the diamond.
In their interior meanings, they are the same but the images are different.
Diamonds are hard, unearthly, celestial, impersonal.
Gold is softer, a matter of relationship.
The self as related.
I think we're lucky to have gold to cope with.
When we see that we have given our spiritual gold to someone to hold for us, there are several ways we might respond.*
So here we need to reflect, as I read, on how we personally have each done this.
*We could go to him or her and say, "The meaning of my life has suddenly appeared in the glow in your eyes.
May I tell you about it?"
This is another way of saying, "I have given you my inner gold.
Will you carry it for me for a while?"
But we rarely see it, and we rarely do things that directly.
Instead we stand across the room, turn our back on him or her, feel totally frightened, stumbling and carrying on in odd ways.
We can banter with each other, speaking all kinds of nonsense.
We joke and laugh, and an animated play goes on.
But when we head back to work, we feel good.
We feel energized and brightened for the day.
And it was not the coffee.
It was the exchange of inner alchemical gold.*
*This exchange of gold is a mysterious process.
It is our gold, but it's too heavy for us.
It is our gold, but it's too heavy for us.
So we need someone to carry it for us for a time.
And that person becomes synonymous with meaning.
We follow him or her with an eagle eye wherever she goes.
His smile can raise us to heavenly heights.
His frown will hurl us to hellish depths.
So great is the power of meaning.*
So have you had experiences like this?
Where someone just is so important, right?
And is it that they have an inherent importance, or an inherent wisdom, or something inherently different from you?
Or have we given them our inner gold?
*Sometimes the exchange of gold takes the form of hero worship.
For a 10-year-old boy, his 12-year-old neighbor is a hero.
And then soon, that changes.
A few years later, when the 10-year-old is 12, he's become the characteristics of his hero.
And then he meets a new hero.
And I remember vividly my own early hero worshiping.
It was so strong.
Slowly and painfully, I've drawn those hero worship projections, this placing of my own potential onto others, back to myself, turning gray in the process.*
There's a great economy of words, this guy.
Turning gray in the process.
*I have become what I was hero worshiping.
I want to tell you this hero worshiping story, and then a little bit more, a few reflections.
When I was 14, I drove with my grandmother to Spokane, Washington, to attend a family funeral.
One of my cousins, a little older than I, had married.
And I saw her husband for the first time.
Instantly, he became my hero.
I was unstable in that period of my life.
My feet didn't work well.
I hadn't really entered the masculine world.
And I'm not greatly endowed in that direction, anyway.
His name was Thor.*
This is like the beginning of the setup for this guy to be a [unclear: "union"].
*His name was Thor.
He was of Norwegian ancestry, in his early 20s, a strong guy, an absolute master of the physical world.
This fellow did something so kind and important for me.
The day after the funeral, he plucked me out of the family gathering and took me into the woods to go hunting.
The first and last hunting I've ever done.
He sensed who I was, what I needed, and at what speed to initiate me.
He knew I had to be told which end of the gun to point where, and he did it so well.
Someone of infinitely high value for me.
I was envious and I was bound to him.
Almost literally.
I placed my feet in his footsteps as we walked through the forest, giddy with his greatness.*
*Suddenly he stopped and he said, "Squirrel on a limb, over there."
Ten or twenty yards away was a squirrel on a pine branch.
"All right," he said, and told me exactly what to do.
"Line this up with the squirrel, pull the trigger gently, don't jiggle the gun, and [unclear: "lose him out of the sight"].
It'll go bang in your ear, don't be afraid."
I did it and of course I thought I'd missed the squirrel.
"Come on," he said.
We went over and lo and behold, I hadn't missed.
On the ground under the limb was a ragged bloody mess of a squirrel.
I was so proud and so horrified at the same time.
I learned in a split second what heroism costs you and what it gives you.
I had become a big man, but I couldn't stand it.
I did not want to shoot squirrels.
We went back home, but I was more pleased than happy.*
*Forty years later I got a letter from my cousin, the same cousin, Thor's wife.
The letter said, "You must be Bob.
My granddaughter brought a book home from her psychology class by Robert Johnson, and I think it must be by you."
I had not seen or heard from my cousin in more than 40 years, but we spoke on the phone and she asked if she could visit for her 60th birthday.
What a wonderful time we had.
She brought a small entourage of people, among whom was a young Thor, the grandson of my hero.
He was the same age I had been when I knew the first Thor, and he was skinny and frightened the way I'd been, quickly going down in the whirlpool of the modern world.
My head was swimming with possibilities.
So I entertained young Thor with a story of my first and only hunting trip, talking about his grandfather and the wonderful day he had given me.*
*Unfortunately, the elder Thor had drunk himself to death, and it was pretty much a failure in his life.
My cousin had divorced him, and he just went down Skid Row.
I didn't like hearing this.
He'd been my hero.
So I told this little guy who hadn't yet said a word to me, "I owe your grandfather an immense debt, and I transfer that debt to you.
I owe you whatever you need from me."
And this boy latched onto me immediately, and I became his hero.
It was a beautiful exchange.
This is alchemical gold.
You put your own gold onto somebody until you've been able to hold it yourself.
As a 14-year-old, I couldn't do what Thor could.
He was 24, 25.
I put my gold onto him.
The gold of masculinity, strength, courage, and independence.
Things I had none of, and he had lots.
And over the course of 40 years, I got my gold back.
I didn't do it by way of guns.
I've never shot a gun since.
I was acutely aware of all this as I sat next to young Thor.
"I have gold for you," I said.
Of course, it was his gold, or it wouldn't work.
I couldn't give him anything, but I could carry his gold if he chose to allow me, and he did.
Because I'm more like him, and he's more like me than either of us is like his grandfather.*
*I've made my way in this world by a series of carriers of gold.
With the aid of heroes, I proceeded in the way that an alpine climber hammers in his piton, secures his rope, pulls himself up to the next piton, and gets ahold of it.
This is how we grow.
Everyone comes to be where he or she is now to some extent through the exchange of gold.*
We'll continue a little more tomorrow with Robert Johnson talking about our responsibility to understand this, so that when we give away our gold, we actually know a little more what we're doing.
And especially when we receive the gold of others, we know what we're receiving and how to hold it in a way that's safe, in a way that's loving, in a way that honors our Buddha gold nature.

So now I'm really wondering if this is a lot of what we've been doing all these years, starting in our particular lives, starting in our particular lineage, starting in the late 50s in the San Francisco area, and people giving their gold to Suzuki Roshi and he in some way trying to give it back on his deathbed, dying too young in 1971 or two.

Different people coming along through karma and circumstance to Berkeley and San Francisco and Bellingham, Washington and Vancouver and all over the world, practicing, trying to understand the nature of this mind and this life and this heart.
But maybe none of us, maybe we weren't doing it exactly the way that we thought.
Maybe we thought, I am me, I am a person with this history and these tendencies and these flaws, and on a good day I'll admit to having a few strengths, and I need a lot of help.
I need a new tool, a new way to be, and it seems like Zen practice is it.
If I practice hard over a long time, I'll little by little improve and grow, some of my foolishness will wear off, maybe I'll learn something.
In a little while into practice it's got to dawn on us that we're actually not doing this individually.
We're an individual amongst other individuals, and we have metaphors like being in a rock tumbler or dirty potatoes in a tub of water, and we start to rub on each other and soften our edges.
But I think still in those models there's an idea of separation.
I'm rubbing my edges off on you and there's a wall between us.
Maybe a permeable wall, maybe a soft wall, maybe an invisible wall that's not always there, but still some separation.
But maybe in that contact it wasn't just that we were smoothed over a little bit, smooth and eased a little bit.
Maybe it was we'd already given each other our gold a long time ago, and we're starting to allow ourselves to receive it back.

And maybe as our teachers mature we start to understand, and of course all of us are teachers in this way, that we're not special or different or wiser, but maybe we've become a little more willing to hold the gold openly, lightly, generously, ready to give it back.
So that's my thought for today, part one.
See if I can develop this in a little more of a clear thesis with a little more of Robert Johnson's help tomorrow.
But think about it, don't think too much.
And of course like all models, if you poke at it, it'll have holes, because no model quite adds up to reality.
The model of the Zen Master doesn't quite hold water.
The model of Inner Gold doesn't quite hold water either.
No model holds water.
But maybe a new model can cast some new light.
Some new light on subtle, complex human dynamics that we will never fully understand.
A couple weeks of contemplating this model is really warming up my heart.
That seems like a good sign.
And it sure made it a whole lot easier to receive that doctor's ridiculous praise.
The glowing Buddha guy in my polo shirt with my flip chart.
So how are we giving and receiving gold?
And sometimes of course, as he'll say tomorrow, that exchange doesn't work too well, right?
The gold is rejected.
The gold is thrown in the mud.
Or they won't give us the gold back.
And we suffer.
So let's continue.
It's an interesting little compressed sesshin.
We do a lot, and nothing at the same time, for three days.
Let's be gentle and quiet as we can be.
If we choose to go out to dinner with friends over the dinner break, let's speak carefully from the heart.
Let's exchange gold instead of banter.
If we choose to go get some food and sit quietly downstairs, that's beautiful too.
And tomorrow, much like today, and then Sunday we'll do some different stuff to close this out.
I want to add to my beginning list of thank yous.
Thank you to Norman for coming up all these years and bringing it back so graciously.
And to all of you for much the same.

verbatim.text: Good afternoon, everybody. This little piece by Wendell Berry keeps coming into my mind, called The Real Work. It may be that when we no longer know what to do, we have come to our real work. And that when we no longer know which way to go, we have come to our real journey. The mind that is not baffled is not employed.

The impeded stream is the one that sings. The mind that's not baffled is not employed. The impeded stream is the one that sings. We don't always like to be impeded, but I guess that's how we sing. So we create this interesting little situation called sesshin so that we can sing. It seems to be like the more complicated, the better.

More impediments and more singing. So I appreciate the many efforts that are happening that this could even be going on. Especially Connie and Talus setting it up and planning it. Both Bobs and John and everybody else in the kitchen. Susan and her crew jumping in to try to serve the food. We've not done the full service, serving the food with servers for a long time,

maybe five years or something like that, nearly than we did once. So it's amazing. It's amazing we can do all this. So I hope you feel at least a little bit baffled.
